content: 1. Lumefantrine, artemether, and dihydroartemisinin (DHA) are not significantly excreted through the kidneys. Therefore, no dose adjustment is recommended for the use of artemether/lumefantrine in patients with renal impairment. 2. No dosage adjustment is necessary for patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment. 3. There is no FDA guidance on the use of artemether and lumefantrine in women of reproductive potential or in males. 4. There is no FDA guidance on the use of artemether and lumefantrine in immunocompromised patients. 5. Limited information is available regarding the administration of artemether and lumefantrine in the drug label. 6. Limited information is available regarding the monitoring of artemether and lumefantrine in the drug label. 7. Limited information is available regarding the compatibility of artemether and lumefantrine with intravenous (IV) administration. 8. There is no information on overdoses of artemether/lumefantrine tablets exceeding the recommended doses for treatment. 9. In cases of suspected overdose, symptomatic and supportive therapy, including ECG and blood electrolyte monitoring, should be provided as appropriate. 10. Artemether/lumefantrine tablets, a fixed-dose combination of artemether and lumefantrine in a 1:6 ratio, act as antimalarial agents. 11. Artemether is rapidly metabolized into an active metabolite, dihydroartemisinin (DHA). 12. The antimalarial activity of artemether and DHA is attributed to the endoperoxide moiety. 13. The exact mechanism by which lumefantrine exerts its antimalarial effect is not well defined. 14. Available data suggest that lumefantrine inhibits the formation of β-hematin by forming a complex with hemin. 15. Both artemether and lumefantrine have been shown to inhibit nucleic acid and protein synthesis. 16. Artemether has the empirical formula C16H26O5 with a molecular weight of 298.4. 17. Lumefantrine has the empirical formula C30H32Cl3NO with a molecular weight of 528.9. 18. Limited information is available regarding the pharmacodynamics of artemether and lumefantrine in the drug label. 19. Following administration of artemether/lumefantrine tablets to healthy volunteers and malaria patients, artemether is absorbed with peak plasma concentrations reached approximately 2 hours after dosing. 20. Lumefantrine, a highly lipophilic compound, begins absorption after a lag time of up to 2 hours, with peak plasma concentrations occurring 6 to 8 hours after administration. 21. Pharmacokinetic parameters for artemether, DHA, and lumefantrine after a single dose (4 tablets) in adult Caucasian healthy volunteers are provided in Table 3. 22. Multiple-dose data after the 6-dose regimen of artemether/lumefantrine tablets in adult malaria patients are provided in Table 4. 23. Food enhances the absorption of both artemether and lumefantrine. 24. In healthy volunteers, the relative bioavailability of artemether increased twoto three-fold, and that of lumefantrine increased sixteen-fold when artemether/lumefantrine tablets were taken after a high-fat meal compared to fasting conditions. 25. Patients should be encouraged to take artemether/lumefantrine tablets with a meal as soon as food can be tolerated. 26. Artemether and lumefantrine are both highly bound to human serum proteins in vitro (95.4% and 99.7%, respectively). 27. Dihydroartemisinin is also bound to human serum proteins (47% to 76%). 28. Protein binding to human plasma proteins is linear. 29. In human liver microsomes and recombinant CYP450 enzymes, the metabolism of artemether is predominantly catalyzed by CYP3A4/CYP3A5. 30. Dihydroartemisinin (DHA) is an active metabolite of artemether. 31. The metabolism of artemether is also catalyzed to a lesser extent by CYP2B6, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19. 32. In vitro studies with artemether at therapeutic concentrations revealed no significant inhibition of the metabolic activities of CYP1A2, CYP2A6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, CYP3A4/CYP3A5, and CYP4A9/CYP3A11. 33. In vitro studies with artemether, DHA, and lumefantrine at therapeutic concentrations revealed no significant induction of the metabolic activities of CYP1A1, CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A4, or CYP3A5. 34. 35. The artemether/DHA AUC ratio is 1.2 after a single dose and 0.3 after 6 doses given over 3 days. 36. This suggests that there was induction of enzymes responsible for the metabolism of artemether. 37. In human liver microsomes and recombinant CYP450 enzymes, lumefantrine was metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to desbutyl-lumefantrine. 38. 39. In vitro, lumefantrine significantly inhibits the activity of CYP2D6 at therapeutic plasma concentrations. 40. Caution is recommended when combining artemether/lumefantrine tablets with substrates, inhibitors, or inducers of CYP3A4, especially antiretroviral drugs and those that prolong the QT interval (e.g., macrolide antibiotics, pimozide). 41. Co-administration of artemether/lumefantrine tablets with CYP2D6 substrates may result in increased plasma concentrations of the CYP2D6 substrate and increase the risk of adverse reactions. 42. Many drugs metabolized by CYP2D6 can prolong the QT interval and should not be administered with artemether/lumefantrine tablets due to the potential additive effect on the QT interval (e.g., flecainide, imipramine, amitriptyline, clomipramine). 43. Artemether and DHA are cleared from plasma with an elimination half-life of about 2 hours. 44. Lumefantrine is eliminated more slowly, with an elimination half-life of 3-6 days in healthy volunteers and in patients with falciparum malaria. 45. Demographic characteristics such as sex and weight appear to have no clinically relevant effects on the pharmacokinetics of artemether and lumefantrine. 46. In 16 healthy volunteers, neither lumefantrine nor artemether was found in the urine after administration of artemether/lumefantrine, and urinary excretion of DHA amounted to less than 0.01% of the artemether dose. 47. No specific pharmacokinetic studies have been performed in patients with either hepatic or renal impairment. 48. There is no significant renal excretion of lumefantrine, artemether, and DHA in healthy volunteers, and while clinical experience in this population is limited, no dose adjustment in renal impairment is recommended. 49. The pharmacokinetics of artemether, DHA, and lumefantrine were obtained in two pediatric studies by sparse sampling using a population-based approach. 50. Pharmacokinetic estimates derived from a composite plasma concentration profile for artemether, DHA, and lumefantrine are provided in Table 4. 51. 52. No specific pharmacokinetic studies have been performed in patients older than 65 years of age.
